entry.title: Portability Challenges in Checking Errors for C String-to-Float Conversion
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | sebsite.pw | discussion

C string-to-float conversion functions like `strtod`, `strtof`, and `strtold` present challenges for portable error detection due to conflicting requirements between the C standard and POSIX. While the C standard uses the `math_errhandling` macro to determine whether to signal errors via `errno` or floating-point exceptions, POSIX mandates that `errno` be set for both overflow and underflow scenarios. This discrepancy leads to inconsistent behavior across different C libraries, such as glibc and musl, where one might set `errno` on invalid input while another does not.

To ensure robust error handling, developers must use the `endptr` parameter to verify if a conversion was successful. For overflow and underflow, error detection requires implementation-specific strategies, such as checking `errno` for `ERANGE`, testing floating-point exception status, or performing manual string analysis, depending on whether the target environment follows POSIX or strict C standards.

entry.title: Spinlocks and the Risks of Priority Inversion
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | matklad.github.io | discussion

Replacing OS-based mutexes with spinlocks, particularly in `#[no_std]` environments, can lead to significant performance and stability issues. These include priority inversion, where high-priority threads spinning on a lock prevent a preempted low-priority lock-holder from regaining CPU time, and deadlocks that occur if an interrupt handler attempts to acquire a lock held by interrupted code.

A demonstration using the `getrandom` crate shows how priority inversion can increase execution times from milliseconds to minutes. Alternatives to spinlocks include using standard mutexes that incorporate an initial spinning period before blocking, delegating state management to the caller, or employing racy initialization techniques.

entry.title: LLVM Compiles Branch-Free Code into Branches on RISC-V
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | 00f.net | discussion

LLVM's optimization of branch-free code for RISC-V can introduce conditional branches, even when developers use bitwise logic in C, Rust, or Zig to ensure constant-time execution. This phenomenon is particularly common in 128-bit integer addition and bitwise selection on 32-bit RISC-V, where the lack of native conditional move instructions often forces the compiler to use jumps.

Such branches can create timing side-channels in cryptographic implementations, undermining security guarantees. While the RISC-V `Zicond` extension provides instructions like `czero.eqz` to facilitate branchless selection, many existing microcontrollers lack this hardware support. Although GCC has demonstrated the ability to emit branchless code for similar operations on some RISC-V targets, LLVM's behavior remains inconsistent across different versions and optimization levels.

entry.title: RwLock vs Lock-free Performance in Read-Heavy Workloads
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | pranitha.dev | discussion

Benchmarks show that lock-free data structures provide significantly higher read throughput and lower latency than RwLock in read-heavy Rust workloads. The performance gap is driven by the atomic overhead required by RwLock to track active readers, which necessitates thousands of atomic increment and decrement operations during a single traversal of a large data block.

Implementing lock-free access via crossbeam-epoch allows a reader to pin a thread to an epoch once, reducing per-item operations to simple atomic pointer loads. While structural changes to the collection still benefit from standard locking, per-element updates are more efficient using epoch-based reclamation.
